title: Building better digital twins
author: @sfiscience
text:
Digital twins mimic real-world systems and evolve alongside them, from bridges and space shuttles to forest fires, tumors and even cities. (image: Rohit Choudhari/Unsplash)October 22, 2026Over the past several years, scientists have been refining ways to model physical structures and systems from bridges and space shuttles to forest fires and tumors. These “digital twins” mimic their real-world counterparts and evolve alongside them. Rather than rely on stationary snapshots, digital twins use ongoing interaction between the physical and virtual systems, enabling “living” simulation and the chance to test out interventions. 

Advances in digital-twin technologies have accelerated across scales, incorporating both small details and big-picture, systemic information into individual models. But how to navigate computational demands, gain public trust, and determine the level of detail that models need to improve lives remain open questions. 

To address breakthroughs and challenges in digital twins, researchers representing aerospace and structural engineering, disaster response, and applied mathematics convened at SFI from September 28 – 30 for the working group “Digital Twins for Complex Systems: Theory and Algorithms.” 

“We’re in the midst of a revolution with digital twins,” says SFI External Professor and Science Board Member Karen Willcox (UT Austin), who co-organized the event. “Today, we're talking about everything from healthcare to airplanes to the management of an entire city.”

With advances in artificial intelligence and growing interest from the National Institutes of Health, National Science Foundation, and Department of Defense, the workshop was ideally timed. “There's been an incredible surge of interest in digital twins, and a lot has changed with AI,” says Willcox. “A lot of developments are coming together all at once.”
 
Medicine has seen a particular groundswell of interest in digital twins. Biological systems are exquisitely complex and require modeling from the genomic level up, incorporating data about a person’s DNA and RNA, metabolism, immune system, and lifestyle to accurately represent a person's body. The potential implications for clinical care are profound.

“The future of cancer includes the right measures, and right interventions, for the right person, at the right time,” says working-group presenter Caroline Chung, Professor of Radiation Oncology & Diagnostic Imaging at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. While clinical trials typically compare a single treatment regimen to the standard of care, digital twins can predict who will respond better to more or less drug, at more or less frequent dosing intervals.

Complex digital twins must incorporate several data types across multiple scales, from individual components to entire systems, requiring expertise and communication across disciplines. “Groups working on each scale are working in silos,” Chung says. Model accuracy is also challenged by missing data, inconsistent data collection and meaning, and the need to adapt dynamically to the breakneck speed of new research findings. 

The working group offered an opportunity to address these challenges. “SFI is a wonderful place for boundary-crossing discussions that you wouldn't normally have the opportunity to have,” says Willcox. “SFI leads in complexity, and as technology advances, more questions will come to the forefront.” 

Willcox and the other working group co-organizers — UT Austin Professor of Mechanical Engineering and Geological Sciences Omar Ghattas and Bart van Bloemen Waanders, a computational scientist at Sandia National Laboratories — are also developing an edited volume on digital twins. The proposed volume will include tutorials, providing students and researchers with a foundation of digital twin methods, as well as perspectives of cutting-edge applications of digital twins.

“How can we make digital twins trustworthy? Explainable?
